after.label: Political history
after.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

after.label: New social history
after.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.

Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996).

before.label: Gender & racial formation
before.description: Examines how gender and race are historically produced through relations of power. Intersectional approaches question treating race, class, and gender separately. Some feminist and gender historians built on British Marxist social history’s attention to labour, culture, and agency while reworking its concepts and questioning gendered exclusions. These exchanges do not define every strand of gender or racial-formation analysis.

added.title: Leopold von Ranke, Die römischen Päpste, ihre Kirche und ihr Staat im sechzehnten und siebzehnten Jahrhundert (1834–1836); Sarah Austin, trans., The Ecclesiastical and Political History of the Popes of Rome (1840).
added.citation: Leopold von Ranke, Die römischen Päpste, ihre Kirche und ihr Staat im sechzehnten und siebzehnten Jahrhundert (1834–1836); Sarah Austin, trans., The Ecclesiastical and Political History of the Popes of Rome (1840).

verification.note: Cambridge reissue description checked for source-centered method and the religious/political scope of the work. Indexed DLA Marbach authority record https://www.dla-marbach.de/find/opac/id/AK01813171/ confirms three-volume original 1834–1836; Folger https://catalog.folger.edu/record/33624 confirms Austin translation, Murray 1840. Linked Cambridge volume is a 2011 reissue. No primary volume or comprehensive reception study read; source criticism predates Ranke.

added.title: Lewis Namier, The Structure of Politics at the Accession of George III (Macmillan, 1929).
added.citation: Lewis Namier, The Structure of Politics at the Accession of George III (Macmillan, 1929).

verification.note: Indexed Manchester institutional account checked for 1929, prosopography through biographies/connections and mixed contemporary reception. NLI catalogue https://catalogue.nli.ie/Record/vtls000399599 confirms original publisher/date. Institutional retrospective does not verify all Namier’s claims about motives or ideological importance; full book and a specific critical reply remain unread.

added.title: Charles Tilly, The Contentious French (Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 1986).
added.citation: Charles Tilly, The Contentious French (Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 1986).

verification.note: Indexed Harvard publisher listing checked for 1986 and the relation of popular collective action to capitalism and state formation; Fayard description of La France conteste (1986), https://www.fayard.fr/livre/la-france-conteste-9782213015767/ , corroborates the question. Tilly’s separately read 1993–1994 essay p. 9 explicitly describes this book’s programme. No full-volume event-data check.

added.title: Charles Tilly, “Social Movements as Historically Specific Clusters of Political Performances,” Berkeley Journal of Sociology 38 (1993–1994): 1–30.
added.citation: Charles Tilly, “Social Movements as Historically Specific Clusters of Political Performances,” Berkeley Journal of Sociology 38 (1993–1994): 1–30.

verification.note: Primary scan downloaded from https://voidnetwork.gr/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/Social-movements-as-historically-specific-clusters-of-political-performances-by-Charles-Tilly.pdf ; pp. 1–3 and 9–10 read. Tilly treats movements as historically specific performances, connects small actions with repertoires, explicitly describes The Contentious French, and limits examples chiefly to Britain/France. He rejects an automatic movement-to-democracy inference and acknowledges this conceptual essay’s limited evidence. No claim of a universal sequence.

added.title: Lynn Hunt, Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (University of California Press, 1984; anniversary edition 2004).
added.citation: Lynn Hunt, Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (University of California Press, 1984; anniversary edition 2004).

verification.note: Publisher description and primary chapter openings read, especially pp. 87 (explicit Geertz use), 123 (symbols/practices), 149 (social identity debate) and 213 (political culture). Contents retain both poetics of power and sociology of politics, including quantitative appendices. The 2004 preface is not treated as 1984 evidence; full chapters and statistical tables were not read. Broad claims of historical invention remain Hunt’s interpretation.

added.title: Ranajit Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983; Duke edition 1999).
added.citation: Ranajit Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983; Duke edition 1999).

verification.note: Duke description and contents checked for insurgent consciousness, dominance/subordination, deliberate peasant political action and the original 1983 versus 1999 edition. James C. Scott wrote the later foreword. No full primary book read; a search-result PDF proved to be Banerjee’s different 2020 book and was excluded. The intervention does not certify homogeneous peasant consciousness or a single path to nationalism.

added.title: Dipesh Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (Princeton University Press, 1989).
added.citation: Dipesh Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (Princeton University Press, 1989).

verification.note: Publisher description and 1989 copyright checked for Calcutta jute-mill workers, culture/consciousness, Marxian categories and criticism of universalizing labor narratives. Primary chapter text was unavailable on the listing; no primary-book or empirical adjudication claimed. Descriptions of workers as preindividualist are attributed and not adopted as neutral classifications.

added.title: Frederick Cooper, Decolonization and African Society: The Labor Question in French and British Africa (Cambridge University Press, 1996).
added.citation: Frederick Cooper, Decolonization and African Society: The Labor Question in French and British Africa (Cambridge University Press, 1996).

verification.note: Publisher-hosted primary Part I introduction, pp. 23–24, read: limits of the free/coerced labor dichotomy, work as a social process and colonial categories obscuring wage workers’ lives. Contents and 1996 print date checked; online 2010 is not original publication. This excerpt does not verify every strike, colonial region or account of decolonization in the volume.

added.citation: Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall, Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class, 1780–1850 (1987).

verification.note: Indexed publisher description checked for original 1987, authors, religion/ideology, economic opportunities and gender in Birmingham and Suffolk/Essex. Indexed primary prologue opening at https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/mono/10.4324/9780203605097-7/prologue-leonore-davidoff-catherine-hall describes family and gender distinctions amid social change; direct pages returned stubs/failure. Linked editions are later reissues. No full-book reading or claim that all middle-class households had identical arrangements.

added.title: Joan W. Scott, “The Evidence of Experience,” Critical Inquiry 17(4) (Summer 1991): 773–797.
added.citation: Joan W. Scott, “The Evidence of Experience,” Critical Inquiry 17(4) (Summer 1991): 773–797.

verification.note: Publisher metadata checked. Primary article transcription consulted at https://studylib.net/doc/13210158/the-evidence-of-experience-author-s---joan-w.-scott-source- , pp. 776–778 and 796–797: recognition of recovery histories, critique of transparent experience, explicit use of Foucault’s genealogy, and retention of experience as something to explain. University-hosted PDF returned 404 and another host had a certificate failure. Transcription/selected passages, not complete scan verification or consensus interpretation.

added.citation: William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959).
